summary: The conditional divorce discussion from 13a reaches its resolution: two rejected formulas (a single get 'on condition your counterpart dies,' then a paired 'counterpart doesn't die'/'you don't enter the synagogue' get) are refuted before the Gemara settles on the working formula, which ties Wife 2's condition to the husband's own act of entering the synagogue - but two scholars raise objections from levirate marriage law that must be addressed. The page then opens a major new topic: the onen (acute mourner) High Priest. A baraita rules he may sacrifice on Yom Kippur but not eat kodshim. R. Yehuda adds 'the whole day,' which Rava interprets as a mitzva to bring the onen KG from home to perform service. Abaye challenges this, and the page closes mid-argument with Rava's position being revised.

display.title: After two rejected attempts, the KG's final formula ties Wife 2's get to his own act
display.oneLine: Two successive rejected formulas - a single conditional get, then a paired 'counterpart doesn't die'/'you don't enter the synagogue' get - are refuted before the Gemara's actual working formula, which ties the second wife's condition to the husband's own act of entering the synagogue.
display.whats: Continuing from 13a: first, to one wife alone he says 'this is your get on condition your counterpart dies.' But perhaps the counterpart does die - the get then becomes valid retroactively, and he is left with no wife at all; this is rejected. Second attempt: he divorces both wives - to one, 'on condition your counterpart does not die,' to the other, 'on condition you do not enter the synagogue on YK.' But perhaps the counterpart does not die and she does not enter the synagogue - then both gets are valid and he ends up with no wife at all; this too is rejected. The Gemara then gives the formula that actually works: to Wife 1, 'on condition your counterpart does not die'; to Wife 2, 'on condition I (the husband) enter the synagogue.' Now if Wife 2 dies, Wife 1's get stands; if Wife 2 lives, Wife 2's get stands only once the husband himself enters the synagogue - his own act, not her compliance. The Gemara adds the retroactivity subtlety: if it looks like Wife 2 is about to die mid-service, he can preemptively enter the synagogue himself, making Wife 2's get retroactively valid. Two scholars then object from levirate marriage law; both are resolved by scriptural amplifications.
display.hint: Why do the first two conditional-divorce formulas fail, and how does making the second wife's condition depend on the husband's own action ensure that exactly one marriage survives?

learning.learnerQuestion: Can a conditional divorce formula be designed so that exactly one of the KG's two wives is ever actually divorced?
learning.coreTension: Every earlier formula on 13a and both attempts tried here either leave the outcome unresolved mid-service or let both conditions hold at once, leaving the KG with no wife; success requires conditions that can never both be true or both be false simultaneously.
learning.coreMove: The first attempt (single get, 'on condition your counterpart dies') is refuted because if the counterpart dies, the get is retroactively valid and he is left with no wife at all. The second attempt (paired 'counterpart doesn't die'/'you don't enter the synagogue') is refuted because both conditions can hold at once. The Gemara's actual solution makes Wife 2's condition the husband's own entry into the synagogue - an act fully under his control, which he can even trigger preemptively to secure retroactive validity.
learning.ahaMoment: Making the second condition the husband's own act, rather than something the wife does, is what finally guarantees mutual exclusivity: he alone controls whether and when he enters the synagogue.
learning.memoryAnchor: First try fails (if the counterpart dies, he's left with no wife at all); second try fails (both conditions about the wives can hold together); final fix ties one condition to the husband's own entry into the synagogue.
learning.learningBlocker: Learners may think one of the two rejected formulas presented first ('counterpart dies' alone, or the paired 'counterpart doesn't die'/'you don't enter the synagogue') is the Gemara's accepted solution. Both are explicitly refuted; the accepted formula replaces the second wife's condition with the husband's own act.

takeaway.text: Tying one wife's condition to the husband's own controllable act, rather than to anything the wife does, is what finally guarantees exactly one divorce is always valid.

argumentFlow.label: First attempt (rejected): single get 'on condition your counterpart dies'
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: To one wife alone, he says: 'This is your get on condition your counterpart dies.' But perhaps the counterpart does die - the get then becomes valid retroactively, and he is left with no wife at all. This formula is rejected.

argumentFlow.label: Second attempt (rejected): paired 'counterpart doesn't die' / 'you don't enter the synagogue'
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: He divorces both wives: to one, 'This is your get on condition your counterpart does not die.' To the other, 'This is your get on condition you do not enter the synagogue on YK.' But perhaps the counterpart does not die and she does not enter the synagogue - then both gets are valid and he is left with no wife at all. This formula is also rejected.

argumentFlow.label: Final formula: Wife 2's condition is the husband's own act
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: To Wife 1: 'This is your get on condition your counterpart does not die.' To Wife 2: 'This is your get on condition I (the husband) enter the synagogue.' If Wife 2 dies, Wife 1's get stands; if Wife 2 lives, her own get stands only once the husband himself enters the synagogue. He can even preempt her death by entering the synagogue beforehand, making her get retroactively valid.

sourceRefs.note: The working formula and its retroactivity explanation

misconceptions.misconception: The paired formula 'counterpart doesn't die' / 'you don't enter the synagogue' is the Gemara's accepted solution.
misconceptions.correction: That formula is explicitly refuted: both conditions can hold at once, voiding both marriages. The accepted formula ties Wife 2's condition to the husband's own act of entering the synagogue.

misconceptions.misconception: The final, accepted solution creates a two-wife situation at some moment.
misconceptions.correction: The final, accepted conditions are mutually exclusive, so only one get can ever be valid at a time.

visualizableElements.item: Rejected second attempt: Wife 1's get triggers if Wife 2 doesn't die; Wife 2's own get triggers if she avoids the synagogue - both conditions can hold together, voiding both marriages.
Accepted formula: Wife 1's get triggers if Wife 2 does not die; Wife 2's get triggers only once the husband himself enters the synagogue - his own controllable act, not hers.

quizSeeds.question: Why does the second conditional divorce formula ('counterpart doesn't die' / 'you don't enter the synagogue') fail?
quizSeeds.answer: Both conditions can hold at the same time - the counterpart doesn't die and the wife simply avoids the synagogue - which makes both gets valid and leaves the KG with no wife at all.

quizSeeds.question: What makes the final, accepted formula succeed where both earlier attempts failed?
quizSeeds.answer: The second wife's condition is tied to the husband's own act - his entering the synagogue - rather than to anything the wife herself does, guaranteeing the two conditions are truly mutually exclusive.

sugyot.finalRuling: The working conditional-divorce formula ties Wife 2's condition to the husband's own entry into the synagogue. Both subsequent yibum objections (covered in yoma-13b-s02) are resolved.
prerequisiteKnowledge: Basic rules of yibum and chalitza
How conditional gitin work with retroactivity

display.title: Two yibum objections, two distinct amplifications override the 'one house' restriction
display.oneLine: Two objections try to import the KG's 'one house' restriction into levirate marriage law; each is resolved by its own distinct scriptural amplification, not a shared expansive reading of 'bayto'.
display.whats: Two parallel objections from levirate marriage law, each raised by a different sage. First: if two yevamot come from the same man (the KG's brother dies childless and both wives face yibum) - the Torah's 'bayto' (singular 'his house') implies only one can do yibum. Second: a betrothed woman (arusah) - does she do yibum or not? The Gemara resolves the first objection through the doubled phrase 'yevamato yevamato' (a ribui, amplification), and the second through the word 'hachutza' ('outside') - two separate amplifications, not a single shared mechanism.
display.hint: Why do the two yibum objections require distinct scriptural answers—'yevamto yevamto' for the two-yevamot case and 'hachutza' for the arusah case—rather than one reinterpretation of 'bayto'?

learning.learnerQuestion: If 'bayto' restricts the KG to one wife on Yom Kippur, doesn't it also restrict yibum to only one of his two wives, and exclude a merely betrothed wife?
learning.coreTension: The KG's 'one house' restriction appears to import itself into the entirely separate law of levirate marriage, but each resulting objection is answered by its own distinct scriptural amplification rather than a shared reinterpretation of any single word.
learning.coreMove: Both objections are resolved by scriptural amplification (ribui) - but each via a different word: the first by the doubled phrase 'yevamato yevamato', the second by 'hachutza' ('outside') - not by any expansive reinterpretation of 'bayto' itself.
learning.ahaMoment: The 'one house' restriction from the KG's Yom Kippur law (Leviticus 16) does not carry over into levirate marriage law (Deuteronomy 25) - the Gemara overrides it for each objection through its own distinct amplification, not by redefining 'bayto'.
learning.memoryAnchor: Two objections, two separate amplifications: 'yevamato yevamato' lifts the two-yevamot problem; 'hachutza' lifts the arusah problem - neither relies on redefining 'bayto'.
learning.learningBlocker: Learners may assume one word must carry one consistent legal scope across the Torah. This sugya shows the same word can be restrictive in one verse and expansive in another, each governed by its own derasha.

takeaway.text: Objections sharing a surface resemblance can be resolved by entirely distinct scriptural derashot: here a doubled-word amplification ('yevamato yevamato') answers the first objection, and a different word's amplification ('hachutza') answers the second - not a single unifying reinterpretation of 'bayto'.

argumentFlow.label: Objection: two yevamot from one man cannot both do yibum
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Asi (or, some say, Rav Avira)
argumentFlow.text: If both wives face yibum ('bayto' - his house, singular), the formula creates an impossible levirate situation: two women, one yibum obligation.

argumentFlow.label: Objection: betrothed wife (arusah) cannot do yibum - resolved by 'outside' (hachutza)
argumentFlow.speaker: Ravina (or Rav Sherevya)
argumentFlow.text: Ravina (or, some say, Rav Sherevya) objects: if so, a betrothed woman (arusah) should not be eligible for yibum either. The Gemara resolves this from the word 'outside' (hachutza) in the yibum verse, which is read to amplify and include the betrothed woman.

sourceRefs.note: Arusah objection and its resolution via 'outside' (hachutza)

misconceptions.misconception: These objections concern the KG's Yom Kippur requirement itself.
misconceptions.correction: They concern how the conditional divorce formula interacts with the separate law of levirate marriage.

misconceptions.misconception: 'bayto' must function the same restrictive way in the yibum context as it does for the KG.
misconceptions.correction: The resolution does not reinterpret 'bayto' itself; each objection is answered by its own distinct amplification - 'yevamato yevamato' for the first objection, 'hachutza' for the second.

visualizableElements.item: The word 'bayto' appearing in two different biblical contexts with different legal scope
KG's 'bayto' (restrictive: exactly one wife) vs. the two distinct yibum-law amplifications ('yevamato yevamato' and 'hachutza') that override that restriction

quizSeeds.question: What is the second objection raised against the backup-wife formula from levirate law?
quizSeeds.answer: An arusah (betrothed woman) may not be eligible for yibum since she hasn't yet entered the husband's household.

sourceRefs.note: Arusah objection and its resolution via 'outside' (hachutza)

quizSeeds.question: How does the Gemara resolve each of the two yibum-law objections to the conditional divorce formula?
quizSeeds.answer: The first objection (two yevamot from one house) is resolved by the doubled phrase 'yevamato yevamato' (a ribui, amplification). The second objection (arusah) is resolved by the separate word 'hachutza' ('outside'). Neither resolution rests on reinterpreting the word 'bayto' itself.

sugyot.finalRuling: Both yibum objections are resolved by their own distinct scriptural amplification (the first via 'yevamato yevamato', the second via 'hachutza'). The two-pronged conditional divorce formula remains valid.
prerequisiteKnowledge: The yibum (levirate marriage) obligation and its conditions

display.title: The onen High Priest: he serves, but he doesn't eat
display.oneLine: The onen KG performs Yom Kippur service despite his mourning, but R. Yehuda's 'kol hayom' addition triggers a contested reading from Rava that Abaye challenges.
display.whats: New topic: the onen (acute mourner - someone whose close relative died that day, before burial). The mishna of Yoma says the KG performs the Yom Kippur service even as an onen. A baraita elaborates: he sacrifices but does not eat the sacred food afterward. R. Yehuda adds: 'kol hayom' (the whole day). Rava interprets this as a mitzva to bring the onen KG from his home to serve, to ease his grief through holy work. Abaye challenges by citing a baraita in R. Yehuda's own name: a priest already mid-service who hears of a relative's death must stop and leave (R. Yosei disagrees). If R. Yehuda himself holds that aninut removes a priest mid-service, how can Rava read his 'kol hayom' as mandating that the onen be actively brought in? Rava revises his explanation.
display.hint: The KG is simultaneously subject to two competing demands: the acute mourner is supposed to stay home and grieve; the KG's unique status requires Yom Kippur service to continue. The baraita resolves in favor of service over mourning - he sacrifices but does not eat.

learning.learnerQuestion: Does the KG's Yom Kippur service obligation override his status as an acute mourner, and what does R. Yehuda's 'the whole day' actually add to that rule?
learning.coreTension: The onen is ordinarily absorbed in mourning and restricted from many activities, yet the KG's unique Yom Kippur role demands continuous service; R. Yehuda's extra phrase 'kol hayom' could mean either an obligation to serve more or a restriction to serve less.
learning.coreMove: The baraita rules the onen KG sacrifices but does not eat kodshim. Rava first reads R. Yehuda's 'kol hayom' as a mitzva to actively bring the onen KG from home to serve all day, but Abaye's challenge, citing a baraita in R. Yehuda's own name that a mid-service priest who hears of a death must leave, exposes an internal contradiction and forces Rava to revise that reading.
learning.ahaMoment: Service overrides personal mourning for the KG on Yom Kippur - the public obligation outweighs private grief. But the prohibition on eating kodshim as an onen remains in force.
learning.memoryAnchor: The onen KG: he serves but doesn't eat. His grief is real but his Yom Kippur duty takes precedence.
learning.learningBlocker: Learners may take Rava's first interpretation as the final word. The sugya explicitly shows it under live challenge from Abaye, with the resolution deferred to 14a.

takeaway.text: Whether R. Yehuda's 'kol hayom' is a mitzva to bring the onen KG in for service or a restriction on his service is unresolved at this point; the debate continues on 14a.

argumentFlow.label: Baraita: onen KG serves but does not eat
argumentFlow.speaker: Baraita
argumentFlow.text: The High Priest who is an acute mourner performs the Yom Kippur service but does not eat the sacred portions afterward. His service is valid; his eating is forbidden.

argumentFlow.label: R. Yehuda: 'the whole day'
argumentFlow.speaker: R. Yehuda
argumentFlow.text: R. Yehuda adds 'kol hayom' to the baraita's ruling, specifying that the onen KG is engaged in service for the whole day.

sourceRefs.note: R. Yehuda's addition (within the same baraita line)

argumentFlow.label: Rava: 'kol hayom' means a mitzva to bring him from home
argumentFlow.speaker: Rava
argumentFlow.text: Rava interprets R. Yehuda's 'kol hayom' as teaching that it is a mitzva to bring the onen KG from his home to the Temple to serve all day, because engagement in holy service alleviates his grief.

argumentFlow.label: Abaye: R. Yehuda's own ruling contradicts bringing the onen in
argumentFlow.speaker: Abaye
argumentFlow.text: Abaye challenges Rava by citing a baraita stated in R. Yehuda's own name: a priest already performing the service who hears that a relative has died stops and leaves (R. Yosei disagrees, holding he finishes) - this is about an ordinary priest, not the KG specifically. If R. Yehuda himself holds that aninut removes a priest from service mid-way, how can Rava read R. Yehuda's 'kol hayom' as mandating that an onen be actively brought in to begin service? Rava must revise his interpretation.

sourceRefs.note: Abaye's challenge (spanning vilna lines 25-28), citing R. Yehuda's own ruling that an onen leaves mid-service

misconceptions.misconception: The onen KG's service is invalid because he is in a state of mourning.
misconceptions.correction: The baraita explicitly rules his service is valid - he sacrifices, though he may not eat the sacred food afterward.

misconceptions.misconception: Abaye's challenge is that 'the Rabbanan' forbid the onen KG from leaving the Temple.
misconceptions.correction: The baraita Abaye cites rules in R. Yehuda's own name (not the Rabbanan's) that a priest mid-service who hears of a death must leave; Abaye's point is an internal contradiction within R. Yehuda's own position, and Rava's reading will be revised; the resolution is deferred to 14a.

visualizableElements.item: The KG in full Yom Kippur garments, performing the avodah while a family member lies unburied - the intersection of public duty and private grief
What the onen KG does (sacrifices, serves) vs. what he cannot do (eat kodshim afterward)

quizSeeds.question: According to the baraita, what can the onen High Priest do on Yom Kippur and what is he forbidden from doing?
quizSeeds.answer: He may sacrifice (perform the Temple service) but may not eat the sacred food (kodshim) afterward.

quizSeeds.question: What challenge does Abaye raise against Rava's interpretation of 'kol hayom'?
quizSeeds.answer: Abaye cites a baraita in R. Yehuda's own name ruling that a priest already mid-service who hears of a relative's death must stop and leave - seemingly contradicting Rava's claim that R. Yehuda mandates actively bringing an onen in to begin service.

sugyot.finalRuling: The onen KG serves on Yom Kippur but does not eat kodshim. Rava's reading of 'kol hayom' as a mitzva to bring the onen KG from home is challenged by Abaye (citing R. Yehuda's own ruling, elsewhere, that an onen priest mid-service must stop and leave) and is revised; resolved on 14a.
prerequisiteKnowledge: The halakhot of acute mourning (aninut) - especially the prohibition on eating kodshim
The KG's unique Yom Kippur service obligation that overrides personal status

glossary.en: Levirate marriage - when a man dies childless, his widow must either marry his brother or be released through chalitza. The conditional divorce formula raises complications for this law.
A betrothed woman (after kiddushin but before nisuin, i.e., before entering the husband's home). Her status regarding levirate marriage is discussed here.
A person in acute mourning from the time a close relative dies until burial. Forbidden from eating kodshim, but the KG's Yom Kippur obligation overrides the acute mourning state.
The whole day - R. Yehuda's addition specifying the onen KG's engagement in Temple service throughout Yom Kippur.

rashiTranslations.en: 'If her counterpart dies' - this one remains, since her get is not a get. 'On condition you do not enter [the synagogue], etc.' -
on Yom Kippur. 'rather, now' - since we said above that 'his house' does not imply two,
two yevamot coming from one man - if he had two wives, not even one of them should
undergo levirate marriage, since 'one house' is written. 'a betrothed woman does not undergo levirate marriage' -
since 'house' is written, and yet you said above that
as long as he has not brought her in, she is not his house.
'Sacrifices as an onen' - since the Torah permitted it, as it is written
(Leviticus 21): 'for his father and his mother he shall not become impure,'
'and from the Sanctuary he shall not leave, and he shall not profane,' etc.
and we expound it in the tractate on the slaughtering of sacred offerings (Zevachim
16a): when his father or mother has died, he does not need to
leave his sanctified state at all, but may remain standing
and sacrificing, since he did not profane his service by doing so, and from this
we derive that a common priest who did not leave has profaned his service.
'And he does not eat' - that only the following was permitted here:
service, but sacred foods are forbidden to an onen, an a fortiori inference
from the more lenient tithe, about which the Torah says
(Deuteronomy 26): 'I have not eaten of it in my mourning.'
'To bring him from his home' - it is a mitzva
that they bring him to the Temple to serve the whole day, in order
to relieve his distress; and this is what Rabbi Yehuda means by 'the whole day' -
he should be engaged in sacrificing. 'now, according to Rabbi'
Yehuda, we actually remove him' - regarding a common priest who is an onen,
even if he already began the service - evidently Rabbi Yehuda
holds stringently regarding the sacrificial service of an onen, and the Rabbis leniently,
but regarding the High Priest they reversed their positions. 'he was
standing and sacrificing' - this refers to a common priest.
This ('to say') is the catchword anticipating 14a's opening comment.
